name: Chroma Noise Ratio
description: Measures the ratio of chromatic noise to luminance noise — real camera sensors produce characteristic chroma-to-luma noise ratios dictated by Bayer CFA sampling and analog amplification. AI generators produce pixel values through neural network computation, yielding fundamentally different noise channel relationships.
algorithm: YCbCr Domain Noise Decomposition + Chroma/Luma Variance Ratio Analysis
mechanism:
In real digital cameras, noise originates from photon shot noise (Poisson-distributed, signal-dependent) and read noise (Gaussian, signal-independent). After Bayer demosaicing, the chroma channels (Cb, Cr) inherently contain more noise than luminance (Y) because: (1) the Bayer CFA captures only one color per pixel requiring interpolation, and (2) the color difference computation amplifies noise. The typical chroma-to-luma noise ratio for authentic photographs is CNR = σ_chroma / σ_luma ≈ 1.3–2.5, depending on ISO and sensor size.

The detector converts the image to YCbCr color space and estimates noise variance separately in each channel using a median absolute deviation (MAD) estimator applied to wavelet detail coefficients (typically Daubechies-4, level 1). The key forensic signals are: (1) **Global CNR** — AI images typically show CNR ≈ 1.0 (equal noise in all channels) or CNR < 1.0 (chroma cleaner than luma), both physically unusual. (2) **CNR spatial consistency** — in authentic photos, CNR varies smoothly with scene illumination; AI images show either perfectly uniform or randomly varying CNR across regions. (3) **ISO-CNR correlation** — if EXIF ISO is available, the estimated CNR should match the expected curve for that sensor/ISO combination; mismatches indicate generation or heavy processing.
parameters:
Color space: YCbCr (ITU-R BT.601)
Noise estimator: MAD on Daubechies-4 wavelet detail coefficients
Expected CNR range (authentic): 1.3–2.5
Suspicious CNR range: < 1.0 or > 4.0
Local analysis window: 64×64 pixels
ISO-CNR lookup: sensor-specific calibration table
accuracy: Moderate — 68-80% accuracy. Strongest at high ISO (≥1600) where chroma noise is prominent; less discriminative at low ISO where all noise is near the sensor floor.
source: Foi, A. et al. (2008). Practical Poissonian-Gaussian Noise Modeling and Fitting for Single-Image Raw-Data. IEEE TIP.
useCase: Detecting AI-generated images through absence of physically realistic chroma noise, verifying sensor origin by matching observed noise characteristics to known camera models, identifying heavy denoising applied to hide artificial generation, and forensic analysis of images claiming specific camera hardware origin.
strengths:
• Based on fundamental sensor physics — CFA interpolation noise is an immutable hardware characteristic
• The CNR metric is simple, interpretable, and fast to compute
• Cross-validates with EXIF ISO metadata when available for stronger authentication
• Particularly effective against early-generation GANs that ignored chroma noise entirely
limitations:
• Modern AI generators that add synthetic noise can approximate natural CNR ranges
• Aggressive chroma denoising (common in smartphone processing) reduces CNR in authentic images
• Low-ISO captures from full-frame sensors have very low noise overall, reducing discriminative power
• Some camera firmware applies different noise reduction to chroma vs. luma channels internally

references.title: Foi, A. et al. (2008). Practical Poissonian-Gaussian Noise Modeling and Fitting for Single-Image Raw-Data. IEEE TIP.
Mahdian, B. & Saic, S. (2009). Using Noise Inconsistencies for Blind Image Forensics. Image and Vision Computing.
